text: Lesson 20's ci.yml for retail-orders-analytics stopped right after dbt deps. The runner has Python, dbt, and dbt's packages installed — but dbt still can't do anything useful, because it has no idea what database to connect to.

On your own laptop, dbt reads connection details from a profiles.yml file that's never committed. A fresh GitHub Actions runner has none of that, so the workflow generates the file itself, every run, with every value — host, user, password, database name — coming from env_var, dbt's function for reading environment variables at run time.

The step that runs dbt uses build, not run and test separately. dbt build runs models, tests, seeds, and snapshots together in dependency order — if a staging model's tests fail, dbt build stops before building anything downstream on top of broken data.

When dbt build hits a failing test, the CI log shows exactly which test failed and how many rows violated it. It's the same output dbt prints locally — CI just captures it and turns the step red, so the pull request shows a failing check before a reviewer even opens the diff.
Before this workflow existed, catching a broken dbt change depended on someone remembering to test locally. Now it's not optional — every pull request gets dbt build run against it automatically.
Next lesson: deploying on merge to main — what happens after a pull request with a passing pipeline actually merges.
